name: Fertile Crescent
what: In the hills from the Levant to the Zagros, foragers turned wild wheat, barley and lentils into crops and herded goats, sheep, cattle and pigs.
why: The first farming and the first villages that grew into towns; farming spread from here to Europe, Egypt and South Asia.

sources.cite: Zeder, M. A., "The origins of agriculture in the Near East", Current Anthropology 52, S221-S235 (2011)
Larson, G. et al., "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies", PNAS 111, 6139-6146 (2014)

name: Yellow River
what: On the loess plain of north China people grew millet, the grain of the first Chinese villages.
why: Millet farming fed the Yangshao and later the Shang.

sources.cite: Lu, H. et al., "Earliest domestication of common millet (Panicum miliaceum) in East Asia extended to 10,000 years ago", PNAS 106, 7367-7372 (2009)

name: Lower Yangtze
what: Wetland foragers of the lower Yangtze slowly turned wild rice into a crop over several thousand years.
why: Rice became the staple of half the world.

sources.cite: Fuller, D. Q. et al., "The domestication process and domestication rate in rice: spikelet bases from the Lower Yangtze", Science 323, 1607-1610 (2009)

name: New Guinea Highlands
what: At Kuk Swamp people dug drains and planted mounds of taro and bananas.
why: An independent invention of farming in the tropics, in an area never touched by the other hearths.

sources.cite: Denham, T. P. et al., "Origins of agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the Highlands of New Guinea", Science 301, 189-193 (2003)

name: Mesoamerica
what: Squash in the Oaxaca caves by 10,000 years ago; maize from wild teosinte in the Balsas valley by 9,000.
why: Maize took millennia to become a big-cobbed staple; it went on to feed the Americas and, after 1492, the world.

sources.cite: Smith, B. D., "The initial domestication of Cucurbita pepo in the Americas 10,000 years ago", Science 276, 932-934 (1997)
Piperno, D. R. et al., "Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico", PNAS 106, 5019-5024 (2009)

name: South-western Amazonia
what: Forest islands in the Llanos de Moxos are full of squash and cassava remains from 10,000 years ago.
why: Amazonia was a cradle of crops, not an untouched wilderness.

sources.cite: Lombardo, U. et al., "Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in Amazonia", Nature 581, 190-193 (2020)

name: Central Andes
what: Around Lake Titicaca and the high puna, people domesticated potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas.
why: High-altitude farming and herding, the base of Tiwanaku and the Inca.

sources.cite: Larson, G. et al., "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies", PNAS 111, 6139-6146 (2014)

name: Western South Asia (Mehrgarh)
what: At Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass, villagers herded humped zebu cattle, tamed locally, and grew barley.
why: The farming roots of the Indus civilisation.

sources.cite: Larson, G. et al., "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies", PNAS 111, 6139-6146 (2014)

name: Sahel and Sudanic savanna
what: Herders of the Green Sahara kept cattle; as it dried, sorghum and pearl millet were domesticated along its southern edge.
why: African crops that later spread to India.

sources.cite: Larson, G. et al., "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies", PNAS 111, 6139-6146 (2014)

name: Eastern North America
what: River-valley foragers in the Midwest domesticated seed plants long before maize arrived.
why: One of the world's independent hearths, often forgotten.

sources.cite: Smith, B. D., "Eastern North America as an independent center of plant domestication", PNAS 103, 12223-12228 (2006)

name: The first dogs
what: Wolves that followed Ice Age hunters became dogs, perhaps in Siberia around 23,000 years ago.
why: The first domestic animal, thousands of years before any crop; where and when is still argued.

sources.cite: Perri, A. R. et al., "Dog domestication and the dual dispersal of people and dogs into the Americas", PNAS 118, e2010083118 (2021)
Janssens, L. et al., "A new look at an old dog: Bonn-Oberkassel reconsidered", Journal of Archaeological Science 92, 126-138 (2018)
